rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrator describes Arab tribes passing Abu Sufyan one by one; al-Abbas identifies the groups as they join Islam.
rows.anchor: ومر عليه القبائل قبيلة قبيلة وهو يقول من هؤلاء وأقول أسلم وجهينة وفلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Sufyan calls Muhammad's growing power kingship, while al-Abbas corrects him that it is prophethood.
rows.anchor: لقد أصبح ملك ابن أخيك عظيما فقلت: ويحك إنها النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hakim ibn Hizam and Budayl ibn Warqa accept Islam and pledge allegiance; Muhammad sends them ahead to invite Quraysh and announce safe places of refuge.
rows.anchor: وجاء حكيم بن حزام وبديل بن ورقاء رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم واسلما وبايعاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad assigns al-Zubayr the emigrants' cavalry and a banner position at al-Hajun, sends Sa'd's Ansar in front, and directs Khalid's force to enter lower Mecca.
rows.anchor: وأمره أن يغرز رايته بأعلى مكة بالحجون وقال له لا تبرح حتى آتيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All forces are told to refrain from fighting unless attacked; four named men and two singers are ordered killed, and the report lists which fugitives are caught and killed.
rows.anchor: وأمرهم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم جميعا أن يكفوا أيديهم ولا يقاتلوا إلا من قاتلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Sa'd announces a day of battle and captivity, Muhammad orders Ali to take the banner and enter Mecca gently.
rows.anchor: أدركه فخذ الراية منه وكن أنت الذي يدخل بها وأدخلها إدخالا رفيقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Kaaba, Muhammad proclaims God's oneness, fulfillment of His promise, and victory, then places prior claims to property, honor, and blood beneath his feet, except the restored offices of Kaaba service and pilgrims' water.
rows.anchor: أنجز وعده ونصر عبده وهزم الأحزاب وحده ألا إن كل مال أو مأثرة ودم تدعى فهو تحت قدمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He declares Mecca sacred by God's decree, with no uprooting its plants, cutting its trees, or frightening its game; lost property may be taken only by someone publicly seeking its owner.
rows.anchor: لا يختلي خلاها ولا يقطع شجرها ولا ينفر صيدها ولا تحل لقطتها إلا لمنشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad rebukes Quraysh for lying, expelling, and harming him, then pardons them; they emerge and enter Islam, and the report explains the Meccans' name al-tulaqaʾ as those released after conquest.
rows.anchor: فاذهبوا فأنتم الطلقاء فخرج القوم فكأنما انشروا من القبور ودخلوا في الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zibara comes to Muhammad, accepts Islam, and recites a poem regretting that he had opened his tongue to falsehood and followed Satan's path.
rows.anchor: وجاء ابن الزبعرى إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأسلم وقال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Muhammad entered Mecca on the conquest day and struck the 360 idols around the Kaaba while reciting that truth had come and falsehood had vanished.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود قال دخل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يوم الفتح وحول البيت ثلاثمائة وستون صنما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Muhammad refused to enter the Kaaba while idols remained, ordered them removed, and condemned images of Abraham and Ishmael shown holding divining arrows.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال لما قدم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى مكة أبى أن يدخل البيت وفيه الآلهة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the hāʾ in Abu Lahab with sukūn; the other readers pronounce it with fatḥ.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير أبي لهب ساكنة الهاء والباقي بفتحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readers give the hāʾ in “dhāt lahab” fatḥ, which fits the verse-end rhymes.
rows.anchor: واتفقوا في ذات لهب أنها مفتوحة الهاء لوفاق الفواصل

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim reads “hammālat al-ḥaṭab” in the accusative; the remaining readers use the nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم حمالة الحطب بالنصب والباقون بالرفع

rows.speaker: البرجمي، أشهب العقيلي، أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Al-Barjami, Ashhab al-Uqayli, and Abu Raja are reported to read “sayuṣlā” with ḍamma on its initial yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وروي عن البرجمي { سيصلى } بضم الياء وهي قراءة أشهب العقيلي وأبي رجاء

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's variant reads “his wife, a carrier of firewood,” with an added preposition before firewood.
rows.anchor: وفي الشواذ قراءة ابن مسعود ومريئته حمالة للحطب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali treats Lahab and Lahab as dialect forms like al-shamʿ and al-nahr; the unanimous fatḥ in “dhāt lahab” supports that vocalization.
rows.anchor: يشبه أن يكون لهب ولهب لغتين كالشمع والشمع والنهر والنهر

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali says nominative “hammālat” attaches to “his wife” and marks a completed action, so it can describe her as a known attribute.
rows.anchor: فمن رفع جعله لقوله { وامرأته } ويدل على أن الفعل قد وقع

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: If “his wife” is coordinated with the subject of “will burn,” Abu Ali prefers not to add an emphatic pronoun after the intervening words; “carrier of firewood” then describes her.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الأحسن أن لا يؤكد لما جرى من الفصل بينهما

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali allows “in her neck” to be a circumstantial phrase, or “his wife” to be a subject with “carrier of firewood” as its description and the neck phrase as predicate.
rows.anchor: ويجوز فيه وجه آخر وهو أن يرتفع امرأته بالابتداء { وحمالة } وصف لها

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Accusative “hammālat” is a disparaging epithet, as if the woman were already notorious for the deed, rather than an identifying description.
rows.anchor: فعلى الذم لها كأنها كانت اشتهرت بذلك فجرت الصفة عليها للذم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Here “rope” means thick rope; the commentary illustrates the word with expressions for a thick-faced man and a thick head.
rows.anchor: وقوله حبل معناه غليظ. رجل حبل الوجه وحبل الرأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root tabb and the noun tabāb mean ruin that leads to destruction; masad is rope made of palm fiber, with amsād as its plural, as a cited poem shows.
rows.anchor: التب والتباب الخسران المؤدي إلى الهلاك والمسد الحبل من الليف وجمعه أمساد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a report from Ibn Abbas through Said ibn Jubayr, Muhammad calls Quraysh from Mount Safa, asks whether they would believe an imminent enemy warning, and declares himself a warner before severe punishment.
rows.anchor: سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab curses Muhammad after the Safa warning; the surah is then revealed, and al-Bukhari includes the report in his Sahih.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو لهب: تبا لك لهذا دعوتنا جميعا فأنزل الله هذه السورة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil explains “perished are Abu Lahab's hands” as his hands and he himself being ruined; hands stand for work because most work is done by them, and the ultimate loss is his soul in the Fire.
rows.anchor: عن مقاتل وإنما قال خسرت يداه لأن أكثر العمل يكون باليد والمراد خسر عمله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes “hand” as an auxiliary expression, like “the hand of time” or “the hand of the year,” with a cited poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: إن اليد هنا صلة كقولهم يد الدهر ويد السنة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says Abu Lahab's hands were emptied of every good; al-Farraʾ reads the first phrase as a curse and the second as a report that he has perished.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: الأول دعاء والثاني خبر فكأنه قال أهلكه الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view treats both phrases as reports: his hands never earned good, and he himself was ruined as well; the verse says he perished in every respect.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الأول أيضا خبر ومعناه أنه لم تكتسب يداه خيرا قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab is Muhammad's paternal uncle, known for intense hostility and opposition; Tariq al-Muharibi recounts seeing him follow Muhammad at Dhu al-Majaz and call him a liar.
rows.anchor: وأبو لهب هو ابن عبد المطلب عم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وكان شديد المعاداة

rows.speaker: طارق المحاربي
rows.claim: Tariq al-Muharibi reports that people identified Muhammad as a prophet and Abu Lahab as his uncle who called him a liar while following him and injuring his legs.
rows.anchor: قال طارق المحاربي: بينا أنا بسوق ذي المجاز إذا أنا بشاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says God uses Abu Lahab's familiar epithet because it was more commonly used than his personal name.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكر سبحانه كنيته دون اسمه لأنها كانت أغلب عليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation avoids calling him Abd al-Uzza, since he is God's servant rather than a servant of al-Uzza.
rows.anchor: لأن اسمه عبد العزى فكره الله سبحانه أن ينسبه إلى العزى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says Abu Lahab was so named for his beauty and bright face, with cheeks that seemed to flame.
rows.anchor: وكانت وجنتاه كأنهما تلتهبان عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wealth and acquisitions did not benefit him or ward off God's punishment; “what he acquired” can be a relative clause with its pronoun omitted.
rows.anchor: أي ما نفعه ولا دفع عنه عذاب الله ماله { وما كسبه }

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes “what he acquired” to mean his child, since a man's child is counted as his earning; Abu Lahab had threatened to ransom himself with wealth and children.
rows.anchor: يعني ولده لأن ولد الرجل من كسبه وذلك أنه قال لما أنذره النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announced fire is Hell, burning with force and intensity; the prediction that Abu Lahab would die an unbeliever came true, proving Muhammad's truth and prophethood.
rows.anchor: تلتهب عليه وهي نار جهنم وفي هذا دلالة على صدق النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وصحة نبوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife is Umm Jamil, daughter of Harb and sister of Abu Sufyan; Ibn Abbas says she carried thorny brush and acacia to injure Muhammad on his way to prayer.
rows.anchor: وهي أم جميل بنت حرب أخت أبي سفيان { حمالة الحطب } كانت تحمل الشوك والعضاة

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas, in a report via al-Dahhak, says she spread thorns across the Messenger's path, which he walked over as one walks on silk.
rows.anchor: قال الربيع بن أنس: كانت تبث وتنشر الشوك على طريق الرسول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، قتادة، مجاهد، عكرمة، السدي
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn Abbas, also attributed to Qatada, Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Suddi, interprets firewood as malicious gossip that kindles hostility; Arabs call this carrying wood against someone.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في رواية أخرى وقتادة ومجاهد وعكرمة والسدي قالت العرب: فلان يحطب على فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem uses “wet firewood” for carrying gossip, supporting the figurative interpretation of firewood as malicious talk.
rows.anchor: ولم يمش بين الحي بالحطب الرطب أي لم يمش بالنميمة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير، أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Said ibn Jubayr and Abu Muslim interpret the wife as carrying sins, like those who bear their loads on their backs.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حمالة الحطب معناه حمالة الخطايا عن سعيد بن جبير وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rope in her neck is made of fiber; the humiliating description degrades and belittles her.
rows.anchor: أي في عنقها حبل من ليف وإنما وصفها بهذه الصفة تخسيسا لها وتحقيرا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says the rope is rough like fiber, hot like fire, and heavy like iron, increasing her punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حبل يكون له خشونة الليف وحرارة النار وثقل الحديد يجعل في عنقها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، عروة بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr say it is a 70-cubit iron chain entering her mouth, exiting behind her, and being wound around her neck in Hell.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وعروة بن الزبير وسميت السلسلة مسدا بمعنى أنها ممسودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word masad describes a chain as twisted rope; the text glosses it as something tightly wound.
rows.anchor: وسميت السلسلة مسدا بمعنى أنها ممسودة أي مفتولة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Said ibn al-Musayyib reports that she owned a splendid jewel necklace and vowed to spend it against Muhammad, so it becomes a punishment around her neck.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أنها كانت لها قلادة فاخرة من جوهر فقالت لأنفقنها في عداوة محمد فيكون عذابا يوم القيامة في عنقها عن سعيد بن المسيب

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت أبي بكر
rows.claim: Asma bint Abi Bakr reports that Umm Jamil came with a stone, reciting insults against Muhammad; she could not see him beside Abu Bakr and left after he denied that Muhammad had insulted her.
rows.anchor: ويروى عن أسماء بنت أبي بكر قالت لما نزلت هذه السورة أقبلت العوراء أم جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary cites the Qur'anic promise of a concealed barrier as a parallel for how Umm Jamil could not see Muhammad.
rows.anchor: كما قال وإذا قرأت القرآن جعلنا بينك وبين الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة حجابا مستورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God diverted the Quraysh's abuse from Muhammad: they insulted Muthammam while his name was Muhammad.
rows.anchor: صرف الله سبحانه عني أنهم يذمون مذمما وأنا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says an angel continually shielded Muhammad from Umm Jamil, accounting for her failure to see him.
rows.anchor: ما زال ملك يسترني عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab remained obligated to believe; God's threat presupposed that he would not believe, so accepting faith would not contradict the prediction that he would enter the Fire.
rows.anchor: أن الإيمان يلزمه لأن تكليف الإيمان ثابت عليه وإنما توعده الله بشرط أن لا يؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh passage shows that repentance is accepted before the moment of despair; only repentance at that late moment is rejected.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دلالة على أنه لو تاب قبل وقت اليأس لكان يقبل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Abu Lahab had asked whether believing would save him from the fire, Muhammad would have answered yes, because the threat's condition would no longer apply.
rows.anchor: لو آمنت هل أدخل النار لكان صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول له لا وذلك لعدم الشرط

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr reads “aḥad Allāh al-ṣamad” without tanwin on the dāl; a report says he paused after “aḥad” and connected it without tanwin, since Arabs did not join such forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو { أحد الله الصمد } بغير تنوين الدال من أحد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali explains the tanwin reading by the meeting of two vowelless consonants, with the first receiving kasra, as in “idhhab idhhab.”
rows.anchor: التنوين من أحد ساكن ولام المعرفة من الاسم ساكن فلما التقى الساكنان حرك الأول

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali explains dropping tanwin by analogy with weak letters, which can be deleted when vowelless before another vowelless letter.
rows.anchor: فلما شابهت حروف اللين أجريت مجراها في أن حذفت ساكنة لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: إسماعيل عن نافع، حمزة، خلف، رويس
rows.claim: Ismail from Nafi, Hamza, Khalaf, and Ruways read kufʾan with a vowelless fāʾ and hamza; Hafs reads kufuwan with a ḍamma on fāʾ and no hamza, while the rest retain hamza and ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ إسماعيل عن نافع وحمزة وخلف ورويس كفؤا ساكنة الفاء مهموزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahad derives from waḥd by changing the initial wāw into hamza; both ahad and wāḥid can function as a noun or an adjective, as the cited verses of poetry illustrate.
rows.anchor: أحد أصله وحد فقلبت الواو همزة ومثله أناة وأصله وناة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural ahadān is used for ahad as an adjective meaning an exalted, incomparable person; expressions like “aḥad al-aḥad” likewise mean to exalt.
rows.anchor: فهذا جمع لأحد الذي يراد به الرفع من الموصوف والتعظيم له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A thing is one in itself if indivisible, but one in an attribute when predicated of something; God's oneness means He alone has essential properties no one shares.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة الواحد شيء لا ينقسم في نفسه أو في معنى صفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣamad means the exalted master to whom needs are directed; other usages call the terminal lord of lordship “the ṣamad.”
rows.anchor: والصمد السيد المعظم الذي يصمد إليه في الحوائج أي يقصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poems by al-Asadi and al-Zibriqan use ṣamad for the master and the endpoint of leadership.
rows.anchor: قال الأسدي: ألا بكر الناعي بخيري بني أسد بعمرو بن مسعود وبالسيد الصمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word muṣammad means intended or sought, and Tarafa applies it to a high, sought-after house.
rows.anchor: وقال رجل مصمد أي مقصود وكذلك بيت مصمد قال طرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kafuʾ, kafīʾ, and kifāʾ all mean an equal or counterpart, as the cited poems from al-Nabigha, Hassan, and another poet demonstrate.
rows.anchor: والكفو والكفىء والكفاء واحد وهو المثل والنظير

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali offers two parses for “Allah”: it can predicate the pronoun “He,” or “He” can be a pronoun of the matter, with Allah as subject and aḥad as predicate.
rows.anchor: يجوز في إعراب الله ضربان أحدهما: أن يكون خبر مبتدأ

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali compares the feminine pronoun of the matter in the verse about disbelievers' staring eyes, since its interpretation contains the feminine noun “eyes.”
rows.anchor: إلا أن هي جاءت على التأنيث لأن في التفسير اسما مؤنثا

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: “Allah” is the subject and ṣamad its predicate, or ṣamad may describe Allah with an omitted “He”; with the matter-pronoun reading, Allah and ṣamad can be successive predicates.
rows.anchor: الله مبتدأ والصمد خبره ويجوز أن يكون الصمد صفة الله

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali takes “lahu” as a non-predicative adverb attached to kāna and kafuwan as its fronted predicate, analogizing the construction to a Qur'anic sentence.
rows.anchor: إن له ظرف غير مستقر وهو متعلق بكان وكفوا منتصب بأنه خبر متقدم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Some Baghdad grammarians instead posit an unexpressed subject in yakun and make kafuwan circumstantial, governed by lahu; Abu Ali resists the analysis unless it is interpreted through the sentence's negation.
rows.anchor: وزعموا أن من البغداديين من يقول أن في يكن من قوله { ولم يكن له كفوا أحد } ضميرا مجهولا

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The negative sense allows ahad to generalize the negation; an affirmative “ahad” could not express this meaning, just as “Zayd except setting out” is not a valid statement.
rows.anchor: فكما أن هذا محمول على المعنى كذلك له كفوا أحد محمول على المعنى

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: A further possible parse makes “lahu” an advanced circumstantial phrase describing the indefinite “kafuwan”; Sibawayh says this is rare in ordinary speech though common in poetry, so the construction is strained but possible.
rows.anchor: فإن سيبويه قال إن ذلك يقل في الكلام وإن كثر في الشعر

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب، جابر
rows.claim: One occasion report says polytheists asked Muhammad to describe or name his Lord, and the surah was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قيل إن المشركين قالوا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم انسب لنا ربك فنزلت السورة عن أبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Amir ibn al-Tufayl asked what Muhammad called people to, then challenged him to describe God as gold, silver, iron, or wood; the surah was revealed, lightning struck Arbad, and Amir later died of a wound.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس. وقيل: جاء أناس

rows.speaker: الضحاك، قتادة، مقاتل
rows.claim: Dahhak, Qatada, and Muqatil report that Jewish scholars asked Muhammad to describe God as in the Torah; the surah was revealed as God's exclusive account or lineage.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جاء أناس من أحبار اليهود إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Ja'far al-Sadiq reports that Jews asked Muhammad to name his Lord; he gave no answer for three days before this surah came down.
rows.anchor: وروى محمد بن مسلم عن أبي عبد الله ع قال إن اليهود سألوا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: A report cited by al-Qadi says Ibn Salam asked Muhammad to describe God; reciting the surah led to Ibn Salam's conversion, which he concealed until Muhammad migrated to Medina.
rows.anchor: وقريب منه ما ذكره القاضي في تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command tells Muhammad to declare to all accountable people that God alone is the one deserving worship; al-Zajjaj says this answers the request to identify God's lineage, and it can also mean that God has no partner or peer.
rows.anchor: هذا أمر من الله عز اسمه لنبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يقول لجميع المكلفين هو الله الذي تحق له العبادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains aḥad as One, with nothing comparable to Him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه واحد { ليس كمثله شيء } عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says God is one in divinity and pre-eternity.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واحد في الإلهية والقدم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view makes God one in the necessary attributes of His essence—existence, knowledge, power, and life—which no other shares as necessary properties.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واحد في صفة ذاته لا يشركه في وجوب صفاته أحد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says God is one in His acts: they are all beneficence, done neither to gain benefit nor to repel harm.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واحد في أفعاله لأن أفعاله كلها إحسان لم يفعلها لجر نفع ولا لدفع ضرر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation says God alone deserves worship because He provides the foundational blessings needed for every other blessing, which no one else can provide.
rows.anchor: واحد في أنه لا يستحق العبادة سواه لأنه القادر على أصول النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahad is stronger than wāḥid: wāḥid can be counted and paired, whereas ahad cannot be divided or have a second, and it excludes even two possible opponents.
rows.anchor: لأن الواحد يدخل في الحساب ويضم إليه آخر وأما الأحد فهو الذي لا يتجزأ

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir reads the command as making the revealed message visible through its letters; “He” points to the unseen God beyond the senses, unlike idols the disbelievers could point to and see.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر الباقر ع في معنى { قل هو الله أحد }

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين علي
rows.claim: Ali reports that al-Khidr taught him in a dream before Badr to invoke “O He, there is no he but He”; Muhammad said this was the greatest name of God, and Ali used it at Badr and Siffin.
rows.anchor: وحدثني أبي عن أبيه عن أمير المؤمنين ع أنه قال رأيت الخضر في المنام قبل بدر

rows.speaker: عمار بن ياسر
rows.claim: Ammar asks Ali about his repeated indirect invocations; Ali explains that they are God's greatest name and the basis of monotheism, then recites the declaration of God's unity.
rows.anchor: فقال له عمار بن ياسر يا أمير المؤمنين ما هذه الكنايات قال اسم الله الأعظم

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين علي
rows.claim: The account ends with Ali reciting the Qur'anic declaration of God's unity and then praying four rakas before noon.
rows.anchor: ثم نزل فصلى أربع ركعات قبل الزوال

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين علي
rows.claim: Ali explains Allah as the deity worshipped and sought by creation, hidden from sight, imagination, and thought.
rows.anchor: الله معناه المعبود الذي يؤله فيه الخلق ويؤله إليه الله المستور عن إدراك الأبصار

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir explains Allah as the one creation cannot comprehend in essence or manner; in Arabic, a-l-h means to be bewildered by something one cannot know.
rows.anchor: وقال الباقر ع: الله معناه المعبود الذي أله الخلق عن إدراك ماهيته

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir defines ahad as the unique individual without a counterpart; tawhid is affirming that uniqueness, and God is distinct, neither derived from nor united with anything.
rows.anchor: والأحد الفرد المتفرد والأحد والواحد بمعنى واحد وهو المتفرد الذي لا نظير له

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir transmits from Zayn al-Abidin, who transmits from Husayn, several senses of ṣamad: ultimate master, everlasting, without a cavity, and without eating, drinking, or sleeping.
rows.anchor: الصمد الذي قد انتهى سؤدده والصمد الدائم الذي لم يزل ولا يزال والصمد الذي لا جوف له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final three descriptions mean God is living without needing food, drink, or sleep.
rows.anchor: المعنى في هذه الثلاثة أنه سبحانه الحي الذي لا يحتاج إلى الطعام والشراب والنوم

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir calls ṣamad the master obeyed by all, with no one above Him to command or forbid Him.
rows.anchor: والصمد السيد المطاع الذي ليس فوقه آمر ولا ناه

rows.speaker: محمد بن الحنفية
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya defines ṣamad as self-subsisting and independent of others.
rows.anchor: وكان محمد بن الحنفية يقول الصمد القائم بنفسه الغني عن غيره

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Other interpreters define ṣamad as transcendent beyond coming-to-be and decay, and indescribable through likenesses.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: الصمد المتعالي عن الكون والفساد والصمد الذي لا يوصف بالنظائر

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين زين العابدين
rows.claim: Zayn al-Abidin says ṣamad has no partner; preserving anything does not burden Him, and nothing escapes Him.
rows.anchor: وسئل علي بن الحسين زين العابدين ع عن الصمد فقال

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali says ṣamad brings any intended thing into being by “Be”; He created things in contrasting kinds and alone has no opposite, form, likeness, or rival.
rows.anchor: قال زيد بن علي ع: الصمد الذي إذا أراد شيئا أي يقول له كن فيكون

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: In a letter answering Basrans who asked about ṣamad, Husayn warns them against speaking about the Qur'an without knowledge and quotes Muhammad's warning that such a speaker faces Hell.
rows.anchor: من قال في القرآن بغير علم فليتبوء مقعده من النار

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: The response says God explains ṣamad through the following negations, beginning that He neither begets nor is begotten.
rows.anchor: وإن الله قد فسر سبحانه الصمد فقال

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: “He does not beget” denies any dense offspring or subtle emergence such as human moods, sleep, dreams, grief, joy, hunger, or hope arising from God.
rows.anchor: لم يخرج منه شيء كثيف كالولد ولا سائر الأشياء الكثيفة التي تخرج من المخلوقين

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: “He is not begotten” means He does not originate from anything, whether dense things produced by elements or subtle faculties emerging from bodily organs.
rows.anchor: أي ولم يتولد من شيء ولم يخرج من شيء كما تخرج الأشياء الكثيفة من عناصرها

rows.speaker: الحسين بن علي
rows.claim: God is not from, in, or on anything; He creates by power, ends what He wills to perish, preserves what He wills to endure, and is the knower of unseen and seen.
rows.anchor: لا بل هو الله الصمد الذي لا من شيء ولا في شيء ولا على شيء مبدع الأشياء

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Ja'far reports that al-Baqir explained ṣamad through its five letters: the alif signifies God's existence, pointing beyond sense perception, as in the testimony of His oneness.
rows.anchor: قال وهب بن وهب: سمعت الصادق ع يقول وفد من فلسطين

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: The letters lāms indicate divinity hidden from perception and description; their inaudible, unwritten? form in speech but visibility in writing illustrates how divine lordship is hidden yet manifested through creation.
rows.anchor: واللام دليل على إلاهيته بأنه هو الله والألف واللام مدغمان لا يظهران على اللسان

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: The visible written letters parallel how God manifests lordship by creating bodies and joining subtle spirits to them, though a person cannot see his own spirit.
rows.anchor: فهو دليل على أن الله سبحانه أظهر ربوبيته في إبداع الخلق وتركيب أرواحهم

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: The ṣād signifies that God is truthful in His being, words, invitation, promise, and intent; the mīm signifies His everlasting true kingship.
rows.anchor: وأما الصاد فدليل على أنه سبحانه صادق وقوله صدق وكلامه صدق

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: The dāl signifies that God's kingship endures and that He creates all created beings, while remaining beyond coming-to-be and extinction.
rows.anchor: وأما الدال فدليل على دوام ملكه وأنه دائم تعالى عن الكون والزوال

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: The Imam laments that he lacks people capable of carrying his God-given knowledge of tawhid, Islam, religion, and law derived from ṣamad; he recalls Ali's unanswered invitation to ask him and warns against siding with those who despair of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: لو وجدت لعلمي الذي أتاني الله حملة لنشرت التوحيد والإسلام والدين والشرائع من الصمد

rows.speaker: عبد خير
rows.claim: Ali explains the surah: ahad is one without numerical counting, ṣamad without division or fragmentation, neither begetting nor begotten rules out inheritance and a divine partner, and no created being is His equal.
rows.anchor: عن عبد خير قال سأل رجل عليا ع عن تفسير هذه السورة فقال قل هو الله أحد بلا تأويل عدد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “He does not beget” as denying parenthood and “He is not begotten” as denying that God is a child.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: { لم يلد } فيكون والدا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says He has no child who could inherit His dominion and did not inherit dominion from another.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { لم يلد } ولدا فيرث عنه ملكه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says begetting would imply need, while being begotten would imply origination and bodily composition; this rebuts claims that Ezra, Christ, or angels are God's children.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { لم يلد } فيدل على حاجته فإن الإنسان يشتهي الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No one is His equal” denies any counterpart or likeness in eternity or other attributes; another interpretation says God has no spouse, indirectly denying offspring.
rows.anchor: أي لم يكن له أحد كفوا أي عديلا ونظيرا يماثله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One structural reading assigns unity to aḥad, justice to ṣamad, denial of parent or child to the next phrase, and denial of every impermissible attribute to the last; this excludes body, substance, accident, place, and direction.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه سبحانه بين التوحيد بقوله { الله أحد }

rows.speaker: بعض أرباب اللسان
rows.claim: Some language experts identify eight forms of association: deficiency, change, multiplicity, number, causation, being caused, shapes, and opposites; each verse negates a pair, producing pure unity.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أرباب اللسان وجدنا أنواع الشرك ثمانية النقص والتقلب والكثرة والعدد

rows.speaker: عمران بن الحصين
rows.claim: Imran ibn Husayn reports that Muhammad asked a returning expedition about its commander Ali, whose sole noted practice was reciting this surah in each prayer; Ali says he loved it, and Muhammad says God loves him for that love.
rows.anchor: وروى عمران بن الحصين أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بعث سرية واستعمل عليها عليا ع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Muhammad used to pause at the end of every verse of the surah.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقف عند آخر كل آية من هذه السورة

rows.speaker: الفضيل بن يسار
rows.claim: Al-Fudayl ibn Yasar says al-Baqir instructed him to recite the surah and repeat “thus is my Lord, God” three times afterward.
rows.anchor: وروى الفضيل بن يسار قال أمرني أبو جعفر أن أقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq means a broad cleft: a sword cleaves a head, and dawn is called falaq because its bright column cleaves darkness.
rows.anchor: أصل الفلق الفرق الواسع من قولهم فلق رأسه بالسيف يفلقه فلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary usage a ghasq is an intruder whose harm surges; the verse means night, when predators and vermin leave their lairs, while related forms describe flowing pus, Hell's discharge, and tears.
rows.anchor: والغاسق في اللغة الهاجم بضرره وهو ها هنا الليل لأنه يخرج السباع من آجامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqaba means entering; a waqba is a hollow because something enters it. Nafth is breath without spittle, unlike tafl, which includes spittle; al-Farazdaq's poem is cited for nafth.
rows.anchor: وقب يقب ومنه الوقبة النقرة لأنه يدخل فيها النفث شبيهة بالنفخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hasid wants another person's blessing removed even without wanting it for himself; envy is blameworthy, whereas ghibta seeks the same blessing without its removal from the other person.
rows.anchor: الحاسد الذي يتمنى زوال النعمة عن صاحبها وإن لم يردها لنفسه فالحسد مذموم

rows.speaker: عائشة، ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report attributed to Aisha and Ibn Abbas says Labid ibn al-Asam bewitched Muhammad and hid a charm in a well; two angels revealed its location, and Ali, al-Zubayr, and Ammar recovered hair, comb remnants, and eleven needle-pierced knots.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة وابن عباس وهذا لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects this as an account of the Prophet being mentally impaired, invoking the Qur'an's rejection of the claim that he was a bewitched man.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يجوز لأن من وصف بأنه مسحور فكأنه قد خبل عقله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author allows that the Jewish man or his daughters may have tried the magic but failed; God exposed their deception and enabled its removal as proof of Muhammad's truth, and their power could not have caused his illness since they would otherwise have killed him and many believers.
rows.anchor: ولكن يمكن أن يكون اليهودي أو بناته على ما روي اجتهدوا في ذلك فلم يقدروا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is to Muhammad, though intended for the whole community: seek refuge with the Lord of dawn, its creator, governor, and bringer forth when He wills.
rows.anchor: هذا أمر من الله سبحانه لنبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم والمراد جميع أمته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، جابر، الحسن، سعيد بن جبير، مجاهد، قتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Jabir, al-Hasan, Said ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Qatada take al-falaq as dawn, whose bright column splits darkness.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس وجابر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view interprets al-falaq as offspring emerging from parents or seeds splitting from plants.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الفلق المواليد لأنهم ينفلقون بالخروج من أصلاب الآباء

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says al-falaq is a pit in Hell whose intense heat its inhabitants seek refuge from; Abu Hamza al-Thumali and Ali ibn Ibrahim also transmit this view.
rows.anchor: عن السدي ورواه أبو حمزة الثمالي وعلي بن إبراهيم في تفسيريهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What He created” is general: refuge is from anything created that can cause evil, including beasts, vermin, and devils.
rows.anchor: وقوله { ما خلق } عام في جميع ما خلقه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid say “when it enters” means when night arrives with darkness; the threat concerns harms that occur at night, when predators, vermin, and wrongdoers are most active.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعلى هذا فيكون المراد من شر ما يحدث في الليل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes ghasq as anything that rushes in bringing harm.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن معنى الفاسق كل هاجم بضرره كائنا ما كان

rows.speaker: الحسن، قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret the “blowers on knots” as sorcerous women; seeking refuge protects religion from their false claims to cure, harm, benefit, serve jinn, and know the unseen.
rows.anchor: معناه ومن شر النساء الساحرات اللاتي ينفثن في العقد عن الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim interprets the women as those who turn men's intentions and decisions toward their own; resolving a decision is a knot, and custom associates undoing knots with blowing.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم: النفاثات النساء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Envy drives a person to inflict harm on the envied, so refuge is sought from the envious person when envy acts.
rows.anchor: فإنه يحمله الحسد على إيقاع الشر بالمحسود فأمر بالتعوذ من شره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading of the danger includes the envious person's own soul and evil eye, which can strike and injure.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أراد من شر نفس الحاسد ومن شر عينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: While discussing the evil eye, the author adduces a supporting hadith that its harm is real.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أراد من شر نفس الحاسد ومن شر عينه فإنه ربما أصاب بهما فعاب وضر وقد جاء في الحديث:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet's she-camel al-Adbaʾ, long undefeated in races, was beaten by a Bedouin's camel; he told the saddened Companions that God lowers whatever He raises in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وروي أن العضباء ناقة للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لم تكن تسبق فجاء أعرابي

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports Muhammad's instruction that someone who sees something admirable should mention God and say “what God wills; there is no strength but through God,” so it is not harmed.
rows.anchor: وروى أنس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: " من رأى شيئا يعجبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Muhammad often sought protection for Hasan and Husayn by reciting these two surahs.
rows.anchor: وروي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان كثيرا ما يعوذ الحسن والحسين ع بهاتين السورتين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the surah gathers all evils and ends with envy to show envy is the basest disposition.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إن الله سبحانه جمع الشرور في هذه السورة وختمها بالحسد

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الدوري عن الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Duri from al-Kisa'i uses imala for “al-nās” in genitive position, but not when it is nominative or accusative; other readers do not use imala.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو الدوري عن الكسائي يميل الناس في موضع الجر ولا يميل في الرفع والنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waswas is inner speech like a hidden sound or whisper, as in al-A'sha's poem about jewelry heard softly when its wearer departs.
rows.anchor: الوسواس حديث النفس بما هو كالصوت الخفي وأصله الصوت الخفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ru'ba's poem uses the verb waswasa for quiet invocation of the Lord of dawn.
rows.anchor: قال رؤبة: وسوس يدعو مخلصا رب الفلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waswasa resembles murmuring; a person overwhelmed by the relevant humor is called muswaswas, and the root has several verbal forms.
rows.anchor: والوسوسة كالهمهمة ومنه قولهم فلان موسوس إذا غلب عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khunus is withdrawal after appearing; the nose's recessed inner parts are also called khunnus because they hide through their lowered shape.
rows.anchor: والخنوس الاختفاء بعد الظهور خنس يخنس ومنه الخنس في الأنف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nās originally was anās, with its hamza dropped, as al-ins and al-unās show; the diminutive nuways replaces the second-letter augmenting alif with wāw.
rows.anchor: وأصل الناس الأناس فحذفت الهمزة التي هي فأو يدلك على ذلك الإنس والأناس

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis makes “from jinn” an appositive to “from the evil of the whisperer,” meaning refuge from the evil of jinn and people.
rows.anchor: قيل إن قوله { من الجنة } بدل من قوله { من شر الوسواس }

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Another analysis makes “from jinn and people” explain the whisperer as an owner or source of whispers; alternatively jinn is the delayed subject of “whispers,” with the pronoun anticipating it.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن من تبين للوسواس والتقدير من شر ذي الوسواس الخناس

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali allows the jinn subject to be understood before its mention, as in Moses' fear within himself, and an omitted object pronoun, as in “the one whom God sent as a messenger.”
rows.anchor: وجازت الكناية عنه وإن كان متأخرا لأنه في نية التقديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes refuge from the whisper itself, which comes from jinn; another means the possessor of whispers, Satan, who retreats when a servant remembers God.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أن معناه من شر الوسوسة الواقعة من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading takes “from jinn and people” as specifying the possessor of whispers; “people” coordinates with the whisperer, so refuge is from both jinn and human tempters.
rows.anchor: وثالثها: أن معناه من شر ذي الوسواس الخناس ثم فسره بقوله من الجنة والناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human tempters may be a person's own self-whispering or people who entice others; Qur'an calls such agents human and jinn devils, and human devils openly pretend to advise while intending harm.
rows.anchor: وفي وسواس الإنس وجهان أحدهما: أنه وسوسة الإنسان من نفسه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Satan contracts when God is remembered and expands over the heart when He is not.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: الخناس الشيطان إذا ذكر اسم الله سبحانه خنس وانقبض

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas ibn Malik reports Muhammad saying Satan rests his snout on Adam's heart, withdraws when God is remembered, and consumes the heart when He is forgotten.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده ما روي عن أنس بن مالك أنه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says khannas means one who repeatedly hides after appearing, unseen by human eyes as he whispers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخناس معناه الكثير الاختفاء بعد الظهور وهو المستتر المختفي من أعين الناس

rows.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Taymi says whispers first arise during ablution.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم التيمي: أول ما يبدو الوسواس من قبل الوضوء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says the whisperer inserts distracting thoughts into hearts through companions who convey them to the chest; this shows that the agents cause harm and can be resisted by seeking refuge.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن معنى قوله { يوسوس في صدور الناس } يلقى الشغل في قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage argues harm comes from those against whom refuge is sought, not from God; if God created evil acts, all harm would be from Him, and the command to seek His protection assures care for the supplicant.
rows.anchor: وفيه دلالة على أنه لا ضرر ممن يتعوذ به وإنما الضرر كله ممن يتعوذ منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is Lord and deity, He is independent of creation; a needy being cannot be God, and the one who knows His sufficiency does not choose evil, making refuge in Him fitting.
rows.anchor: ولما وصف سبحانه نفسه بأنه الرب الإله الغني عن الخلق فإن من احتاج إلى غيره لا يكون إلها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سنان
rows.claim: Abd Allah ibn Sinan reports Abu Abd Allah's instruction to say inwardly “I seek refuge in the Lord of dawn” when reciting that surah, and likewise “I seek refuge in the Lord of people” when reading this one.
rows.anchor: وروى عبد الله بن سنان عن أبي عبد الله ع قال: إذا قرأت

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Ja'far ibn Muhammad reports Muhammad's teaching that each believer has two inner ears: an angel whispers into one and the whispering retreating Satan into the other; God supports the believer through the angel.
rows.anchor: وروى العياشي بإسناده عن أبان بن تغلب عن جعفر بن محمد قال قال رسول الله
